entities.name: Saint Thomas Church, Strasbourg
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Church of Saint Thomas (Église Saint-Thomas de Strasbourg, German: Thomaskirche) in Strasbourg is one of the most historically and artistically significant Evangelical Lutheran churches in France — a collegiate church founded in the 12th century, converted to Lutheranism in 1524 (one of the first churches taken over in Strasbourg's Reformation under Martin Bucer), home to the celebrated Silbermann organ (played by Albert Schweitzer and the principal instrument of the Strasbourg Bach tradition), and containing the extraordinary Maréchal de Saxe tomb (by Jean-Baptiste Pigalle, 1777), one of the greatest sculptural monuments in France.

Saint Thomas was a collegiate church (staffed by a chapter of canons rather than a parish priest) — one of Strasbourg's most important pre-Reformation ecclesiastical foundations. Its early Reformation conversion in 1524 made it the center of Strasbourg's Protestant theological life; it housed the theological faculty that trained Reformation-era ministers. Albert Schweitzer, the Nobel Peace Prize-winning humanitarian, musician, and theologian, was a choirmaster and organist at Saint Thomas in the early 20th century and his recordings on the Silbermann organ produced the definitive interpretations of Bach's organ works for their era.

The Maréchal de Saxe monument (the tomb of Maurice, Marshal of Saxony, erected posthumously by Louis XV's mistress Madame de Pompadour's influence) is one of the most remarkable Baroque sculptural programs in France — depicting the marshal striding toward death while France and his allies weep, Death opens the tomb, and allegorical figures of his opponents celebrate. Its placement in a Protestant church (by a Catholic king's decree for a Protestant marshal) is a historical curiosity reflecting the marshal's fame.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Saint Thomas Church Strasbourg — site of Strasbourg's first Reformation conversion (1524), home of the Silbermann organ that Albert Schweitzer used for his defining Bach recordings, and containing Pigalle's extraordinary Maréchal de Saxe monument — is one of France's most historically and artistically significant Protestant churches.
